strongest_angle: Examining NASA Earth Observatory satellite findings and Landsat data from 1984 to 2023 showing that global mangrove forests shifted from long-term decline to a widespread expansion beginning around 2010 across Asia, Australia, and South America.

key_facts.fact: NASA Earth Observatory researchers analyzing Landsat imagery collected between 1984 and 2023 discovered a global mangrove forest rebound beginning around 2010, led by expansion in Asia, Australia, and South America.

Between the 1980s and 2010, global mangrove forests shrank from around 155,000 square kilometers to 152,000 square kilometers, representing a loss equal to half of Rhode Island according to Anthropocene Magazine.

Yale E360 reported that new mangrove growth between 2010 and 2023 covered approximately 3,200 square miles, outpacing losses across locations from Louisiana to Myanmar, West Africa, and northern Australia.

Researchers including Zhen Zhang, Nicholas J. Murray, Xiao-Peng Song, Pete Bunting, and Thomas A. Worthington published findings in Science showing that global mangrove loss rates reduced substantially from the 1980s to 2023 while gains increased markedly.
